passage:
Monday, cold and foggy. The teacher pulls bibs from a bag without looking: red for Farida, blue for Vikas. Farida hugs her red bib to her chest.
Wednesday. At practice Farida shouts, "Red is the fastest! Red is the best!" She will not share crayons with the blue table. "Blue is slow," she tells Vikas. Vikas sticks out his tongue.
Friday, sports day. Red loses the sack race. Farida's lip wobbles. Then the teacher mixes everyone up for the tug of war, and Farida pulls right next to Vikas, both of them yelling.

qa.q: What colour bib did Farida get?
qa.a: Red.

qa.q: How does Farida feel when red loses the sack race?
qa.a: She feels sad and disappointed 😢, her lip wobbling, because she had decided red was the best team.

qa.q: What did the mixed tug of war do, and why does it help?
qa.a: Putting everyone into one team let Farida and Vikas pull side by side, softening the red-versus-blue feeling.

qa.q: How does Vikas feel when Farida calls blue slow?
qa.a: Vikas feels annoyed and sticks out his tongue, though he was put in blue by chance just as she was put in red.

grounding: Children given bibs at random quickly decide their own colour is best, until a mixed game brings them together.

subtype: Pride in the group and dislike of rivals [Actor]
passage:
House coach's note, Sports Week, January
Samir (Class 5, Green House) has been our loudest supporter all week. He painted his cheeks green and cheered every race until his voice cracked. On Thursday Yellow House won the relay by a hand's length. Samir went quiet, kicked the fence and sat with his face in his knees, as if he had lost something of his own. By lunch he and two friends were chanting "Yellow cheats!" at the Yellow runners. I took him aside, told him his pride in Green was lovely to see, and asked what the Yellow anchor might feel hearing that chant. He shrugged, then said, "Bad." He agreed to shake the winners' hands at the closing ceremony, and he did.
Deepika, house coach

qa.q: Which house won the relay?
qa.a: Yellow House.

qa.q: What does Samir kicking the fence suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt personally hurt and angry, as if Yellow's win were a loss of his own.

qa.q: What did Deepika do next, and why was it a good step?
qa.a: Deepika praised Samir's pride in Green but asked him to imagine the Yellow anchor's feelings, then had him shake the winners' hands, turning mockery back into respect.

qa.q: How might the Yellow runners feel hearing the chant?
qa.a: They would likely feel hurt and insulted on a day they had fairly earned a win.

grounding: A child proud of his school house feels personally hurt when rivals win and slips into mocking them.

passage: It was Christmas week, the colony strung with lights, and Urmila had been glowing for three days since her school won the inter-school debate trophy. She had posted the team photo four times. Then on Sunday her cousin Pooja, who went to the rival convent school, said at lunch, "Your school only won because the judges were from your side." Urmila put down her fork. "Take that back. We practised every day for two months. At least our school doesn't buy trophies." The table went silent. Pooja muttered, "It was a joke." Urmila stormed out to the balcony, cheeks hot, feeling as if Pooja had insulted her, not a debate team she had never even been on.

qa.q: What trophy did Urmila's school win?
qa.a: The inter-school debate trophy.

qa.q: Why did Pooja's joke hurt Urmila so much?
qa.a: Urmila's pride was tied to her school, so she felt personally insulted and angry, even though she had never been on the debate team.

qa.q: What could Urmila try once she calms down on the balcony?
qa.a: She could apologise for the trophy-buying jibe, tell Pooja the joke stung, and remind herself that her worth is not the school's win.

qa.q: How might Pooja see the lunch argument?
qa.a: Pooja may feel she only made a light joke and be shocked and a bit hurt by the fierce reply about her own school.

grounding: A teenager's mood rides on her school's win, and a joke about the school feels like an insult to her.

passage: This Chhath I noticed something about myself. In my Pune college hostel I'm "the Bihari one". When someone jokes about Bihar I feel it in my spine, and I'll defend litti chokha to anyone. But in the robotics lab nobody cares where I'm from; I'm Reena who fixes motor drivers, and I feel like an engineer first. On match nights in the common room I'm just a screaming cricket fan, hugging Swati from Kerala when our side hits a six. Then I went home for Chhath, stood at the ghat with Maa before sunrise, and suddenly I was a daughter, a village girl and a hostel student with a strange new accent, all at once. It helped to see that no single label is all of me. Next time someone says "the Bihari one", I'll let it be one part, not the whole.

qa.q: What does Reena fix in the robotics lab?
qa.a: Motor drivers.

qa.q: How does Reena feel when someone in the hostel jokes about Bihar?
qa.a: Reena feels defensive and stung, feeling it right in the spine, because in the hostel being Bihari comes forward.

qa.q: What does Reena decide about the "Bihari one" label, and why is it wise?
qa.a: To treat it as one part, not the whole, so no single label takes over how Reena or anyone else sees Reena.

qa.q: What might Swati see in Reena on match nights?
qa.a: Swati sees a fellow fan sharing the joy of every six, not "the Bihari one" or an engineer.

grounding: A student feels Bihari in the hostel, an engineer in the lab and a cricket fan in the common room, and sees that no single label is the whole self.

passage: Sunaina, you asked why your Tanvir mama never lets anyone at the shop talk about "those people". Let me tell you. I was twenty-five, waiting outside the maternity ward at the government hospital for your cousin Rubel to be born. The corridor was split: Bengali-speaking fathers on one bench, Hindi-speaking ones on the other, and I sat with my own without thinking. I even felt a little proud of our bench. Then the power went out at midnight. A Bihari man, Ramdeo, had the only torch. He walked it down the whole corridor so every nurse could see, then shared his flask of tea with our bench first. After that we weren't two benches. We were one row of frightened fathers. When I opened the shop, I hired Ramdeo's nephew. I still love our Bengali songs. I just don't need anyone else to be less.

qa.q: Who had the only torch when the power went out?
qa.a: Ramdeo, a Bihari man.

qa.q: How did young Tanvir feel sitting on the Bengali bench at first?
qa.a: He felt at home and a little proud of "our bench", sitting with his own people without thinking.

qa.q: What choice in the story shows the us-them line loosening?
qa.a: Tanvir later hired Ramdeo's nephew at his shop, treating an outsider fairly while still loving Bengali songs.

qa.q: What might Ramdeo have felt, walking the torch down the corridor?
qa.a: He probably felt anxious like every waiting father, and wanted every mother and baby to be safe, not just those from his side.

grounding: A young father notices the pull to favour his own group in a hospital corridor, finds a wider shared identity as fathers and later treats outsiders fairly.

subtype: Feeling poor next to a friend [Actor]
passage: Tanuja, come sit, the Ganpati lights are on. You're sulking about Mitali's new tablet, na? Your Irawati Mausi was ten once, in this same festival. My friend Shalini rode up to our pandal on a shiny red bicycle with gears, and a mobile phone on a string round her neck. I had a bicycle too, a fine old blue one from my cousin. We had enough rice, enough books, a modak for everyone. And yet that night I cried into my pillow as if I had nothing. Nothing in my house had changed. Only what I was looking at had changed. My Aai didn't scold. She asked me to list three things I had loved that day before Shalini arrived. I got to five.

qa.q: What did Shalini have round her neck?
qa.a: A mobile phone on a string.

qa.q: Why did young Irawati cry into her pillow?
qa.a: She felt sad and poor next to Shalini, even though nothing in her house had changed; the hurt came from comparing.

qa.q: What choice in the story helped young Irawati, and why?
qa.a: Her Aai asked her to list three things she had loved that day, which turned her attention back to what she really had.

qa.q: How might Shalini have felt riding up to the pandal on the new bicycle?
qa.a: Shalini probably felt excited and proud, with no idea that the new things were making a friend feel poor.

grounding: A child who has enough at home feels poor after seeing a friend's new bicycle and phone, because of comparison rather than real lack.

passage:
Shashthi. Arnab's new kurta is nice, cotton, sky blue. Then Indu from his class walks into the pandal in a silk one with mirror work, and Arnab tugs at his collar all evening.
Ashtami. The half-yearly results arrive on the class group. Arnab has 84 percent, his best ever. Indu has 91. Arnab mutes the group and tells Ma the paper was "unfair". At dinner he picks at his luchi. "Why do some people get everything?"
Dashami. He carries his little cousin through the crowd to watch the immersion. The boy on his shoulders shrieks with joy at everything. Arnab catches himself smiling. His 84 is still his best. The kurta is still nice. Only looking at Indu had made them feel small.

qa.q: What percentage did Arnab get in the half-yearly exam?
qa.a: 84 percent, his best ever.

qa.q: Why does Arnab tell Ma the paper was "unfair"?
qa.a: He feels cheated and envious comparing his 84 with Indu's 91, even though 84 is his best ever.

qa.q: What could Arnab try when the comparison starts next time?
qa.a: He could compare his marks with his own past results, as he does when he remembers 84 is his best, rather than with the classmate a step ahead.

qa.q: How might Ma see Arnab's mood at dinner?
qa.a: Ma might be puzzled and a little worried that her son calls his best result unfair and asks why some people get everything.

grounding: A teenager with a decent kurta and his best marks feels cheated comparing himself with a classmate a step ahead.

passage:
"Happy New Year, man." Eshaan held out a paper cup of cold coffee on the hostel terrace.
"Happy for who?" Mridul said. "Seniors from our branch got twelve-lakh offers two years ago. Same college. Same syllabus. I topped two semesters and got nothing."
"The market dropped, Mridul. Half the batch..."
"The computer science lot still got placed. Every one of them. It's like the companies decided we don't count."
"You sound like they owe you."
"They do! I did everything the seniors said. That was the deal."
"There was never a deal, yaar. There was a good year."
Silence. Fireworks cracked over the city.
"I know," Mridul said at last, quieter. "I just don't know what to do with being this angry."
"Start with the alumni list tomorrow? I'll help."

qa.q: What offers did the seniors from Mridul's branch get?
qa.a: Twelve-lakh offers, two years ago.

qa.q: Why is Mridul so bitter on New Year's Eve?
qa.a: He feels angry and cheated, believing he was owed the kind of job his seniors got after following their path.

qa.q: What small step does Eshaan suggest, and why could it help?
qa.a: Starting with the alumni list tomorrow, because it turns the anger into a concrete action instead of waiting for what feels owed.

qa.q: How does Eshaan see Mridul's idea of a "deal"?
qa.a: Eshaan sees it as a mistake: there was never a deal, only a good year for the seniors.

grounding: A graduate who expected a job like his seniors got feels bitter and owed, especially as another branch gets placed.

passage:
Subject: Mood in support after the field-team allowance
Hi Gurleen,
Since the field sales team got the new travel allowance and laptops last month, the mood in my support team has soured. Nobody's pay changed; our salaries were checked against the market in April and are fair. But at lunch I hear "we're the second-class team" and "they're the favourites". Two people have stopped joining the Friday call. I don't think it's greed. I think they can't see why one group got something and they didn't.
My plan: at Thursday's team meeting I'll explain exactly what the allowance covers (fuel and client travel) and why support doesn't qualify, and share the written criteria for all perks. I'd also like us to ask whether support needs anything specific, like better headsets.
Could you join, so it isn't just my opinion?
Amandeep

qa.q: What did the field sales team get last month?
qa.a: The new travel allowance and laptops.

qa.q: What does Amandeep think is behind the team's resentment?
qa.a: Amandeep feels concerned but understanding, believing it is not greed but hurt at not seeing why one group got something and they didn't.

qa.q: Why is Amandeep's plan likely to help?
qa.a: Explaining what the allowance covers, sharing written criteria and asking what support needs makes fairness visible, so people feel less left behind.

qa.q: How do the support team members seem to see the allowance?
qa.a: They see it as proof that they are the second-class team and the field team are favourites, even though their own pay is fair.

grounding: A manager notices resentment when one team gets perks although everyone is paid fairly, and plans clear criteria and an honest explanation.

passage:
Wednesday, late.
Sarika got the team lead role today. I clapped in the meeting, then went to the washroom and stood there fuming, fists tight. We joined on the same day. She's good, but I'm good too.
On the bus home I did the thing my old coach taught me: two lists.
What I actually have: a job I mostly like, a client who asks for me by name, my own rent paid, Ma's voice every Sunday.
What I can control: asking my manager what the lead role needs, finishing the analytics course, speaking up in reviews.
Then I looked back. Two years ago I cried after my first presentation. Today I ran one without notes.
I still want to lead a team. I just don't want envy choosing my mood.
Tomorrow I'll congratulate Sarika properly. Pallavi, you can want more and still be glad for her.

qa.q: What did Sarika get today?
qa.a: The team lead role.

qa.q: What was Pallavi feeling in the washroom after the meeting?
qa.a: Pallavi felt envious and angry, standing there with tight fists, because they had joined on the same day.

qa.q: Which of Pallavi's steps turns envy into something useful?
qa.a: Listing what can be controlled, like asking the manager what the role needs and finishing the course, keeps the ambition while letting go of the fuming 🙂.

qa.q: How might Sarika feel if Pallavi congratulates her properly tomorrow?
qa.a: Sarika would likely feel warm and supported by a colleague who joined the same day, rather than sensing a silent rivalry.

grounding: A young adult fuming at a peer's promotion lists what they have and can control and compares with their own past, keeping ambition without envy.
